Mechanism of action

Metoclopramide work as antiemetic (anti nausea and vomiting) by antagonizing central Dopamine D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (which is part of the medulla oblongata of the brainstem) => this will inhibit nausea and vomiting triggered by most stimuli

At high doses, metoclopramide also antagonizes serotonin 5 HT3 receptors which also contribute to its antiemetic effect

Metoclopramide also work as a prokinetic medication, prokinetic means drug that enhance motility of the upper GIT; Metoclopramide achieves that by:

It blocks the peripheral Dopamine D2 receptors => increase the amplitude and duration of esophageal contractions, this also increases the tone of the lower esophageal sphincter and relaxes the pyloric sphincter and duodenal bulb

increasing the muscarinic activation which also lead to increase GI motility

It also work as serotonin 5 HT4 receptor agonist which also lead to increase GI motility

metoclopramide prokinetic effect also contribute to its antiemetic effect

Therapeutic uses

FDA approved for:

Treatment of GERD in patients who fail to respond to life style modification and PPI

Treatment of nausea and vomiting in diabetic gastroparesis

IV metoclopramide is used in Treatment of nausea and vomiting in chemotherapy patients

It is used off label

Prophylactic prevention of nausea and vomiting in postoperative patients when nasogastric suctioning is contraindicated or unavailable

Treatment of nausea and vomiting and reduces headache intensity in acute migraines attacks in emergency settings

Treatment of nausea and vomiting in Hyperemesis gravidarum in pregnant patients, according to ACOG it is indicated for refractory cases because it can cross placenta and lead to methemoglobinemia and extrapyramidal signs in neonates

Treatment of nausea and vomiting in critically ill advanced liver disease patients

Treatment of Diamond-Blackfan anemia, metoclopramide hypothesized to stimulate erythropoiesis through induction of prolactin release in these patients

Pharmacokinetics

It is available as oral, rectal, intraperitoneal, nasal spray, IM and IV formulations, the last two options reserved for severe cases

Oral formulation is well absorbed with peak plasma concentrations reached after 1 to 2 hr. of oral administration

Half life is 4.5- 9 hr.

It is metabolized by CYP2D6, glucuronidation and sulfate conjugation and excreted through urine

Adverse effects

Metoclopramide may lead to extrapyramidal side effects due to the central blocking of the dopamine D2 receptors; extrapyramidal symptoms include:

  • Tremor: shaking movements
  • Rigidity (hypertonia): resistance to passive movement
  • Dystonia: sustained muscle contractions (most common drug induced movement disorder)
  • Akathisia: inability to remain still

Dyskinesia: involuntary repetitive muscle movement, that occur with long term treatment; that is why metoclopramide advised to be used for less than 12 weeks

Metoclopramide may lead to hyperprolactinemia which is also caused by the central dopamine D2 receptor blockade; hyperprolactinemia may present as gynecomastia, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, impotence and hypogonadism

Metoclopramide may lead to neuroleptic malignant syndrome; which Present as autonomic disturbance in form of muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, high blood pressure, sweating and myoglobinemia; it is a serious complication with 20% mortality rate; to treat this, drug should be discontinued and dantrolene (help to relax muscles) is administered

In patients with G6PD deficiency or nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency, metoclopramide can cause methemoglobinemia and sulfhemoglobinemia because metoclopramide increases oxidative stress

Metoclopramide can increase the serum aldosterone level leading to fluid retention and volume overload due to activation of RAAS by metoclopramide

Metoclopramide may lead to development of a purpuric rash not related to thrombocytopenia; it subsides once the drug is discontinued

Metoclopramide may lead to laxative effect in addition to its prokinetic effect leading to diarrhea (less common and occur mostly in children)

Metoclopramide may affect the mood and lead to psychiatric adverse effects because of its antagonist effect on 5 HT3 and agonist effect on 5 HT4 => agitation, irritability, abnormal behaviors, panic disorders, major depressive disorder and agoraphobia (rare)

Drug- Drug interactions

Reduced efficacy of dopamine agonists e.g. bromocriptine and cabergoline since metoclopramide blocks dopamine receptors

Concurrent administration of metoclopramide with antipsychotic drugs should be avoided because both lead to Dopamine receptors blockage and this would lead to additive effects and side effects (especially neuroleptic malignant syndrome)

Efficacy of metoclopramide is reduced if it is taken with anticholinergics or opioids because both slow gastric emptying

Oral metoclopramide increase serum aspirin levels due to increased absorption of aspirin (may lead to salicylate toxicity); same can happen with bupropion and cyclosporin ;; it also may decrease the absorption of some other medication e.g. digoxin

Metoclopramide shouldn’t be used with CYP2D6 inhibitors medications (e.g. fluoxetine) because this would inhibit metoclopramide metabolism => higher drug levels => higher risk for side effects

Contraindications

Metoclopramide is contraindicated in patient with history of hypersensitivity reactions to the medication

It is contraindicated in suspected bowel obstruction or perforation, and in GI hemorrhage

It is also contraindicated in patients with clinical depression

It is contraindicated in patients with seizure disorders because it lower the seizure threshold

It is contraindicated in Parkinson disease

It is contraindicated in patients with pheochromocytoma because it enhance the release of catecholamines and may lead to hypertensive crisis

US boxed warning: metoclopramide can cause tardive dyskinesia (serious movement disorder), therefore avoid treatment for longer than 12 weeks
